'''Peter J. Rousseeuw''' (born 13 October 1956) is a Belgian [[statistician]] known for his work on [[robust statistics]] and [[cluster analysis]]. He obtained his PhD in 1981 at the [[Vrije Universiteit Brussel]], following research carried out at the [[ETH]] in Zurich, which led to a book on [[Robust statistics#Influence function and sensitivity curve|influence functions]].<ref>{{cite book |last1=Hampel |first1=Frank|last2=Ronchetti|first2=Elvezio|last3=Rousseeuw|first3=Peter J.|last4=Stahel|first4=Werner|title=Robust statistics: the approach based on influence functions |date=1986 |publisher=Wiley |location=New York |isbn=978-0-471-73577-9|doi=10.1002/9781118186435}}</ref> Later he was professor at the [[Delft University of Technology]], The Netherlands, at the [[University of Fribourg]], Switzerland, and at the [[University of Antwerp]], Belgium. Next he was a senior researcher at [[Renaissance Technologies]]. He then returned to Belgium as professor at [[KU Leuven]],<ref name=":0">{{cite web|title=ROBUST@Leuven – Departement Wiskunde KU Leuven|url=https://wis.kuleuven.be/stat/robust|website=Ku Leuven|access-date=21 December 2015}}</ref> until becoming emeritus in 2022. His former PhD students include Annick Leroy, Hendrik Lopuhaä, Geert Molenberghs, Christophe Croux, [[Mia Hubert]], Stefan Van Aelst, Tim Verdonck and Jakob Raymaekers.<ref>{{cite web|website=The Mathematics Genealogy Project |title=Peter Rousseeuw |url=http://www.genealogy.ams.org/id.php?id=36126}}</ref>

== Research ==

Rousseeuw has constructed several frequently used methods.<ref name=":0" /><ref>{{cite web|title=Peter Rousseeuw |url=https://scholar.google.com/citations?user=5LMM6rsAAAAJ&hl=en|website=Google Scholar |access-date=21 December 2015}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|title=Peter Rousseeuw|url=https://www.researchgate.net/profile/Peter-Rousseeuw|website=ResearchGate|access-date=6 November 2022}}</ref> He proposed the [[Least Trimmed Squares]] method<ref name=":1">{{cite journal|last1=Rousseeuw|first1=Peter J.|title=Least Median of Squares Regression|journal=Journal of the American Statistical Association|date=1984|volume=79|issue=388|pages=871–880|doi=10.1080/01621459.1984.10477105|citeseerx=10.1.1.464.928}}</ref><ref>{{cite journal|last1=Rousseeuw|first1=Peter J.|last2=Van Driessen|first2=Katrien|title=Computing LTS Regression for Large Data Sets|journal=Data Mining and Knowledge Discovery|date=2006|volume=12|issue=1|pages=29–45|doi=10.1007/s10618-005-0024-4|s2cid=207113006}}</ref><ref>{{cite book|last1=Rousseeuw|first1=Peter J.|last2=Leroy|first2= Annick M.|title= Robust Regression and Outlier Detection |title-link= Robust Regression and Outlier Detection |date=1987|publisher=Wiley|location=New York|isbn=978-0-471-85233-9|edition=3. print.|doi=10.1002/0471725382}}</ref> and [[S-estimator]]s<ref>{{cite book|first1=P.|last1=Rousseeuw|first2=V.|last2=Yohai|title=Robust and Nonlinear Time Series Analysis |chapter=Robust Regression by Means of S-Estimators |volume=26|date=1984|pages=256–272|doi=10.1007/978-1-4615-7821-5_15|series=Lecture Notes in Statistics|isbn=978-0-387-96102-6}}</ref> for
[[robust regression]], which can resist [[outliers]] in the data. This work led to his book [[Robust Regression and Outlier Detection]] with Annick Leroy.

He also introduced the Minimum Volume Ellipsoid and Minimum Covariance Determinant methods<ref>{{cite journal|last1=Rousseeuw|first1=Peter J.|last2=van Zomeren|first2=Bert C.|title=Unmasking Multivariate Outliers and Leverage Points|journal=Journal of the American Statistical Association|date=1990|volume=85|issue=411|pages=633–639|doi=10.1080/01621459.1990.10474920}}</ref><ref>{{cite journal|last1=Rousseeuw|first1=Peter J.|last2=Van Driessen|first2=Katrien |title=A Fast Algorithm for the Minimum Covariance Determinant Estimator|journal=Technometrics|date=1999|volume=41|issue=3|pages=212–223|doi=10.1080/00401706.1999.10485670}}</ref>
for robust scatter matrices.

With Leonard Kaufman he coined the term [[medoid]] when proposing the [[k-medoids]] method<ref>{{cite conference|author1=Kaufman, L. |author2=Rousseeuw, P.J. |title=Clustering by means of Medoids|series= In the book Statistical Data Analysis Based on the L1–Norm and Related Methods, edited by Y. Dodge, North-Holland|date=1987|pages=405–416}}</ref> for [[cluster analysis]], also known as Partitioning Around Medoids (PAM).
His [[silhouette (clustering)|silhouette]] display<ref>{{cite journal|last1=Rousseeuw|first1=Peter J.|title=Silhouettes: A graphical aid to the interpretation and validation of cluster analysis|journal=Journal of Computational and Applied Mathematics|date=1987|volume=20|pages=53–65|doi=10.1016/0377-0427(87)90125-7|doi-access=free}}</ref> shows the result of a cluster analysis, and the corresponding silhouette coefficient is often used to select the number of clusters. The work on cluster analysis led to a book titled Finding Groups in Data.<ref>{{cite book|last1=Kaufman|first1=Leonard|last2=Rousseeuw|first2=Peter J.|title=Finding groups in data: an introduction to cluster analysis|date=1990|publisher=Wiley|location=New York|isbn=978-0-471-87876-6 |doi=10.1002/9780470316801}}</ref> 
Rousseeuw was the original developer of the [[R package]] ''cluster'' along with Mia Hubert and Anja Struyf.<ref name=cluster>{{citation|url=https://cran.r-project.org/web/packages/cluster/index.html|title=cluster: "Finding Groups in Data": Cluster Analysis Extended Rousseeuw et al.|date=2021-04-17|access-date=2021-05-27}}</ref>

The [[Robust measures of scale#Absolute pairwise differences|Rousseeuw–Croux scale estimator]] <math>Q_n </math><ref>{{cite journal|last1=Rousseeuw|first1=Peter J.|last2=Croux|first2=Christophe|title=Alternatives to the Median Absolute Deviation|journal=Journal of the American Statistical Association|date=1993|volume=88|issue=424|pages=1273|doi=10.2307/2291267|jstor=2291267}}</ref> is an efficient alternative to
the [[median absolute deviation]] (see [[robust measures of scale]]).

With Ida Ruts and [[John Tukey]] he introduced the [[bagplot]],<ref>{{cite journal|last1=Rousseeuw|first1=Peter J.|last2=Ruts|first2=Ida|last3=Tukey|first3=John W.|title=The bagplot: a bivariate boxplot|journal=The American Statistician|date=1999|volume=53|issue=4|pages=382–387|doi=10.1080/00031305.1999.10474494}}</ref> a
bivariate generalization of the [[boxplot]].

His more recent work has focused on concepts and algorithms for statistical depth functions in the settings of multivariate, regression<ref>{{cite journal|last1=Rousseeuw|first1=Peter J.|last2=Hubert|first2=Mia|title=Regression Depth|journal=Journal of the American Statistical Association|date=1999|volume=94|issue=446|pages=388|doi=10.2307/2670155|jstor=2670155}}</ref> and functional data, and on robust [[principal component analysis]].<ref>{{cite journal|last1=Hubert|first1=Mia|last2=Rousseeuw|first2=Peter J|last3=Vanden Branden|first3=Karlien|title=ROBPCA: A New Approach to Robust Principal Component Analysis|journal=Technometrics|date=2005|volume=47|issue=1|pages=64–79|doi=10.1198/004017004000000563|s2cid=5071469}}</ref>  His current research is on == Recognition ==
Rousseeuw was elected Member of [[International Statistical Institute]] (1991), Fellow of [[Institute of Mathematical Statistics]] (1993), and Fellow of the [[American Statistical Association]] (1994). His 1984 paper on robust regression<ref name=":1">{{cite journal|last1=Rousseeuw|first1=Peter J.|title=Least Median of Squares Regression|journal=Journal of the American Statistical Association|date=1984|volume=79|issue=388|pages=871–880|doi=10.1080/01621459.1984.10477105|citeseerx=10.1.1.464.928}}</ref> has been reprinted in ''Breakthroughs in Statistics'',<ref>{{cite book|last1=Kotz|first1=Samuel|last2=Johnson|first2=Norman|title=Breakthroughs in Statistics |volume=III|date=1992|publisher=Springer |location=New York |isbn=978-0-387-94988-8|doi=10.1007/978-1-4612-0667-5}}</ref> which collected and annotated the 60 most influential papers in statistics from 1890 to 1990. He became an [[ISI highly cited researcher]] in 2003, and was awarded the Jack Youden Prize (2018, 2022) and the [[Frank Wilcoxon Prize]] (2021), the [[George Box Medal]], and the Research Medal of the International Federation of Classification Societies. In 2024, he received the [[Gottfried E. Noether Awards|Gottfried E. Noether Distinguished Scholar Award]] of the [[American Statistical Association]].

== [[Rousseeuw Prize for Statistics]] ==
From 2016 onward, Peter Rousseeuw worked on creating a new biennial prize, sponsored by him.<ref>{{cite web|title=The Rousseeuw Prize for Statistics|url=https://www.rousseeuwprize.org|website=Rousseeuw Prize|access-date=1 November 2022}}</ref> The goal of the prize is to recognize outstanding statistical innovations with impact on society, and to promote awareness of the important role and intellectual content of statistics and its profound impact on human endeavors. The award amount is 1 million US dollars, similar to the Nobel Prize in other fields. The first award was presented in 2022.
